idiom_name: ServiceGroup/Service for ordered startup and shutdown + swift-nio control listener + Task cancellation
implementation_notes: Server-side Swift takes its control surface from the server packages: swift-service-lifecycle defines Service and ServiceGroup so the process starts components in order, waits for the first to finish and then shuts the rest down, releasing resources before exiting - a stop command is a graceful ServiceGroup shutdown rather than a kill. swift-nio provides the non-blocking channel and handler stack on which a dedicated control listener (a small admin route or a bounded line protocol) is added, and structured-concurrency cancellation propagates shutdown to the component's async work; OSLog/os_signpost and swift-metrics carry the status half. No framework supplies a management bus, so the command vocabulary and its authorisation are the project's own; the classic message-bus form is justified only when the fleet already runs a broker with a Swift client.
pitfalls: Structured concurrency makes stop cooperative: unless every long-running loop checks Task.isCancelled or awaits a cancellation point, cancelling the group does not stop the component - blocking work must be wrapped in withTaskCancellationHandler.

A control listener sharing the public port or route is reachable by every client; swift-nio does not authenticate for you, so the control channel needs its own port (or unix socket) plus token or mTLS checks.
ServiceGroup shuts down when the first service returns, so a control service that exits early silently tears down the whole process - control loops must only end on an explicit shutdown signal.

variants.name: Distributed actors as a cluster control plane
variants.idiom_name: distributed actor + distributed funcs over an ActorTransport (Swift Distributed Actors cluster)
variants.implementation_notes: With distributed actors, remote control is a language feature rather than a channel convention: a component exposes distributed funcs (suspend(route:), snapshot()), another node resolves the actor reference through the receptionist or an ActorIdentity, and the call becomes a message over the ActorTransport - the Swift Distributed Actors cluster library supplies one built on swift-nio, with membership and failure detection. Cluster events and watchTermination give the status half (a terminated signal when a watched actor or its node goes down), and the compiler enforces that distributed parameters and results are Codable. Use this when the system is genuinely multi-node Swift; a single-node service is simpler with ServiceGroup plus an admin route.
pitfalls: Remote calls fail for network reasons: distributed funcs must be throwing, and the caller must treat 'no answer' as unknown state rather than assuming the command was rejected or applied.
Cluster membership is eventually consistent: acting on a single terminated signal can race with a node rejoining, so destructive decisions should be based on quorum/membership state.
Resolving an actor identity is not a liveness check - a reference to a dead node resolves fine and only fails on the first call.
